sentences: A canvas three metres wide, filled edge to edge with colour and line.
Before you search the picture for what it depicts, simply let this noisy chorus of colour wash over you for a moment.
The Russian-born painter Wassily Kandinsky made this large canvas in 1913, while living in Munich.
He prepared more than thirty studies for it, and the final painting is said to have taken only four days.
Today it hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow.
Let us begin at the top.
Sharp wedges, round blots and eye-like rings fly off in every direction.
At first glance, everything seems to explode outward and scatter, and nothing stays still long enough to be named.
Yet just left of centre lies a dark vortex of deep blue and black.
Inside it sits a small oval that looks almost like an eye.
Look again at the whole, and you will notice that all the colour patches and lines of the picture turn around this dark core.
Below the vortex, black lines cut across the canvas.
Thick and thin, straight and curved, they cross each other and set up a rhythm.
Like notes on a score, they pull your eye along.
In the lower left corner, heavy black curves are layered over one another.
Set against pinks and greens, the shape seems to resemble something, yet it never quite lets you name it.
Toward the bottom centre, yellow, blue and pink patches collide.
Warm colours leap forward while cool ones fall back, and the surface seems to pulse.
It is colour in lively conversation with colour, with no object standing in between.
Move your eyes to the right, and a broad pale field opens up, crossed by large sweeping curves.
Compared with the turmoil on the left, it feels like a pause for breath.
Even this canvas has fast and slow movements.
Art historians read in it the Flood, the Resurrection, the Last Judgment and the Garden of Eden, dissolved into one another.
In this view, apocalyptic figures from his earlier pictures grew more and more abstract until they arrived here.
Kandinsky believed colour moves the soul directly, the way music does.
That is why he gave the work a musical title, Composition, a word that also means writing music.
He reserved it for pictures that grew from a feeling slowly matured.
Painting a feeling rather than a thing, this work became a landmark of what abstract art could do.
Kandinsky called it the most complex piece he ever painted.
Step back now, and listen: what kind of sound does it make for you?
